glossa.text:
« There was a man in the land of Hus. » ((GREG. in Job, tom. I.)) By Job, Christ is designated, that is, the head and the body: therefore, after the history, having seen in the head what we are to believe, let us see from the body what by seeing we are to hold.

GREG. ((Ibid.)) Job in the land of Hus, etc., *as far as* afterwards also cunning things were gathered.

 ((ID., ibid.)) The person is first described as fitting, before his combat is told, so that such a one may be seen able to conquer. « Simple. » It is needful that the cunning of the serpent instruct the simplicity of the dove, and that simplicity temper the cunning; whence the Spirit appeared in a dove and in fire, because they who are full of him so serve the meekness of simplicity that against evils they are kindled with zeal for uprightness.

« Fearing God. » Solomon: « He who fears God neglects nothing ((Eccle. VII)). »

((Ibid.)) Likewise Solomon: « He who offends in one thing shall lose many good things ((Eccle. IX)). » Those animals are called lawful, that is, clean according to the law, which both chew the cud and divide the hoof: of which the camels have the one, but the other is lacking to them, and so they both agree with the law and differ from it.

notes.text: Trusted — I have committed my cause and affairs to thee.
For — I dare appeal to thee, because thou knowest I have a deep sense of thy loving-kindness, by which I have been led to love and obey thee.
Sat — Continued with them. I have been so far from an imitation of their wicked courses, that I have avoided their company. Vain - With false and deceitful persons. Go in - Into their company.
Compass — Approach to thine altar with my sacrifices: which I could not do with any comfort, if I were conscious of those crimes, whereof mine enemies accuse me.
House — Thy sanctuary and worship. honour - Thy glorious and gracious presence.
Gather not — Do not bind me up in the same bundle, or put me into the same accursed condition with them.

Standeth — I stand upon a sure and solid foundation, being under the protection of God's promise, and his almighty and watchful providence. Congregations - I will not only privately, but in the assemblies of thy people celebrate thy praise. David declares his confidence in God, ver. 1-3. His desire to be in the house of God, ver. 4-6. He prays for light and salvation, ver. 7-12. And exhorts others to wait upon God, ver. 13, 14. A psalm of David.

glossa.text:
*A psalm.* ((CASS.)) This psalm admonishes that the fellowships of the wicked be shunned, and that we be joined to the just, because from living together manners are formed.

*Judge.* ((AUG.)) Because after mercy, etc., *as far as* they are carried off by the wind of pride.

 ((CASS.)) *Judge:* it is not the presumption of a just man, but the certainty of God's mercy, which he shews there in hoping in the Lord; then, I shall not be weakened.

*In innocence.* ((AUG.)) Not that of angels, but such as is of men.

*Prove me.* ((CASS.)) That is, first look upon my strength, etc., *as far as* I regard not merits, but the mercy which has made me such.

((CASS.)) *Prove me.* But do thou prove me in temptations, that no sin remain, etc., *as far as* lest any man murmur about them.

*Burn my reins.* ((ID.)) With the fire of thy word, the *heart* with the heat of the spirit. *Heart* for thoughts, *reins* for delights.

*Mercy.* ((CASS.)) Which suffers not that we be tempted above our strength; or that very burning is mercy, not harshness

*I have been well pleased in truth.* ((AUG.)) He to whom his own lie is displeasing, and who himself is pleasing along with her and in her.

*I have not sat.* ((CASS.)) *I have been well pleased* in truth, because I have not sat. *I have hated,* which is to shun evils. *And I will wash,* which is to do right things.

*The vain.* ((CASS.)) *The vain* are they who labour about perishable things; the wicked are heretics, who pervert the Scriptures: those seek superfluous things, these poisonous.
*Of the malignant.* ((ID.)) Who do evils to their neighbours.

*I will wash.* ((AUG.)) By doing penance. *And the altar,* I will adorn my mind with virtues, or faith, because there is no place of true sacrifice outside the catholic Church.

 *Among the innocent.* ((AUG.)) Conversing; *that I may hear* from them, that is, that I may learn with what voice thou art to be praised; or, *that I may hear:* Come, ye blessed of my Father.
*The voice of praise* of the Holy Ghost, who teaches to praise thee.

*Lord.* ((CASS.)) He asks that he be not mingled with the wicked in the judgment, because it is not with them, but with the house of God, that he agrees.

*I have loved the beauty.* ((CASS.)) These things therefore will I do, because I have loved to make for thee a comely house, and a place wherein thou mayest dwell in glory, that I may take in something of the glory and the essence of God.

*Destroy not.* ((CASS.)) And if for the present thou sufferest us to be together, destroy us not together.

 ((CASS.)) Destroy me not in time to come *with the wicked,* with whom here I have no fellowship.
*Their right hand,* ((AUG.)), that is, if they do any good, etc., *as far as* let mercy accompany in all things, which thou owest, because:

*Foot,* that is, affection, which is wont easily to slip, *hath stood* unmoved against all scandals, stretching beyond, and persisting *in the right way.* And because thou so redeemest in the churches, I will bless.

*It hath stood.* ((CASS.)) Even though shaken on every side, or confounded by scandals.

notes.text: The proposition and sum, 5-9

The treatise itself. We have a perfect author of salvation, who suffered for our sake, that he might be, (1.) a merciful, and (2.) a faithful, (3.) high priest,. 10-13 These three are particularly explained, his passion and consummation being continually interwoven

1. He has the virtues of an high priest a. He is faithful, iii.1 Therefore be ye not unfaithful iv.13 b. He is merciful, 15 Therefore come to him with confidence v.3

2. He is called of God an high priest. Here, a. The sum is proposed, 4-10 With a summary exhortation 11- vi. 20 b. The point is copiously,

1. Explained. We have a great high priest,

1. Such as is described in the hundred and tenth Psalm After the order of Melchisedec, vii. 1-19 Established by an oath, 20-22 For ever, 23-28

2. Therefore peculiarly excellent-Heavenly, viii. 1-6 Of the new covenant, 7-13 By whom we have an entrance into the sanctuary ix. 1 x. 18

2. Applied. Therefore,

1. Believe, hope, love 19-25 These three are farther inculcated, a. Faith, with patience, 26-39 Which, after the example of the ancients,. xi.1 xii.1 And of Christ himself, 2, 3 Is to be exercised, 4-11 Cheerfully, peaceably, holily, 12-17 b. Hope, 18-20 c. Love, C.xiii. 1-6

2. In order to grow in these graces, make use of The remembrance of your former, 7-16 The vigilance of your present, pastors, 17-19 To this period, and to the whole epistle, answers The prayer, the doxology, and the mild conclusion, 20-25 There are many comparisons in this epistle, which may be nearly reduced to two heads:

1. The prophets, the angels, Moses, Joshua, Aaron, are great; but Jesus Christ is infinitely greater

2. The ancient believers enjoyed high privileges; but Christian believers enjoy far higher. To illustrate this, examples both of happiness and misery are everywhere interspersed: so that in this epistle there is a kind of recapitulation of the whole Old Testament. In this also Judaism is abrogated, and Christianity carried to its height. HEBREWS

Who sat down — The third of these glorious predicates, with which three other particulars are interwoven, which are mentioned likewise, and in the same order, Colossians i, 15, 17, 20. Who, being - The glory which he received in his exaltation at the right hand of the Father no angel was capable of; but the Son alone, who likewise enjoyed it long before. The brightness of his glory - Glory is the nature of God revealed in its brightness. The express image - Or stamp. Whatever the Father is, is exhibited in the Son, as a seal in the stamp on wax. Of his person - Or substance. The word denotes the unchangeable perpetuity of divine life and power. And sustaining all things - Visible and invisible, in being. By the word of his power - That is, by his powerful word. When he had by himself - Without any Mosaic rites or ceremonies. Purged our sins - In order to which it was necessary he should for a time divest himself of his glory. In this chapter St. Paul describes his glory chiefly as he is the Son of God; afterwards, ver. 6, &c., the glory of the man Christ Jesus. He speaks, indeed, briefly of the former before his humiliation, but copiously after his exaltation; as from hence the glory he had from eternity began to be evidently seen. Both his purging our sins, and sitting on the right hand of God, are largely treated of in the seven following chapters. Sat down - The priests stood while they ministered: sitting, therefore, denotes the consummation of his sacrifice. This word, sat down, contains the scope, the theme, and the sum, of the epistle.

This verse has two clauses, the latter of which is treated of, ver. 5; the former, ver. 13. Such transpositions are also found in the other epistles of St. Paul, but in none so frequently as in this. The Jewish doctors were peculiarly fond of this figure, and used it much in all their writings. The apostle therefore, becoming all things to all men, here follows the same method. All the inspired writers were readier in all the figures of speech than the most experienced orators. Being — By his exaltation, after he had been lower than them, chap. ii, 9. So much higher than the angels - It was extremely proper to observe this, because the Jews gloried in their law, as it was delivered by the ministration of angels. How much more may we glory in the gospel, which was given, not by the ministry of angels, but of the very Son of God! As he hath by inheritance a more excellent name - Because he is the Son of God, he inherits that name, in right whereof he inherits all things His inheriting that name is more ancient than all worlds; his inheriting all things, as ancient as all things. Than they - This denotes an immense preeminence. The angels do not inherit all things, but are themselves a portion of the Son's inheritance, whom they worship as their Lord.

glossa.text: *Of old.* It is not new. *God,* who is unchangeable then and now. *Speaking.* He says: *speaking,* in the present, because what was then is even now. *To the fathers.* That is, to those who are fathers to us in flesh and in the worship of God. *In the prophets.* For not they themselves, but God in them. *In divers manners.* That is, many times to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the rest, and often to the same men. *And in many ways.* Because now by dreams, as to Daniel: now by an open voice, as to Moses: now by inward inspiration, as to David.

*In the Son,* who is greater than the prophets. For he is the fulfiller and sanctifier of the prophets. Thus then he is a prophet, in that he is also the Lord of the prophets. So too Christ is an angel, in that he is also the Lord of the angels. *He appointed* unchangeably. *Heir of all things,* that is, possessor of every creature. For Jacob is no longer the portion of the Lord, and Israel his part: but absolutely all the nations of the world.

*Who being the brightness of his glory,* etc. Here he commends Christ according to his divine nature, showing him coeternal and coequal with the Father, and of the same substance with him, but other in person.

*The figure of his substance.* Behold, otherwise, personally, as a figure from him whose figure it is. But equal, because not unlike, as he himself says: *The Father is in me;* and: *He that seeth me, seeth my Father also ((Joan. XIV))*. Note that these names, namely light, glory, are sometimes referred to the divine nature, sometimes to the person. And when they are referred to the person; they are referred now to the Father, now to the Son. For we say: The Father is light, and the Son is light. Likewise the Father is glory, the Son glory, and these two are one glory and one light, not two. And the Son is called glory of glory, as light of light, and beginning of beginning, and God of God, yet not two gods, but one, not two beginnings, but one. But brightness and figure, as image also, are properly referred to the person of the Son and are said relatively.

 *And upholding all things,* etc. It was said above that through him he made all things. Here he now attributes to him the sum of authority, from this, that with authority he governs and holds together all things. For as all things were created by him, so through him, who is unchangeable, they are preserved. For the omnipotence of the Creator is the cause of subsisting to every creature, and if that power should at any time cease from ruling the things it founded, at once the form and nature of all things would fall together.

*Purgation.* After he has shown the excellence of him by whom he created and governs all things, here he commends the kindness of his humility. For he puts us in mind of the cross and the resurrection and the ascension, where he says: *He sitteth,* etc. *On high.* In saying this, he does not shut God up in a place: but shows the man Christ loftier than all and more eminent than all. So also by the right hand he did not give God a shape, but showed the likeness of honour. For he that hath confessed *Confessus*; read *consessus*, "the sitting together" shows nothing else but equality of honour.

*So much better.* Yet in the psalm he says: *He was made a little less than the angels ((Psal. VIII))*. Here he is said to be better than the same. And as that was said according to his human nature, so this too could be understood to have been said according to the divine, were it not that *made* is added, by which it is opened that here he speaks of him according to the flesh. For according to that whereby he is acknowledged consubstantial with the substance of the Father, he was not made, but born: the discourse therefore is of him according to his human nature, according to which he was both less than the angels in his passion, and greater and better also in the fulness of grace, of which the angels themselves also receive by measure.

*A more differing name.* While he was mortal, he had a differing name, because the angels ministered to him. After he was immortal, more differing still. And because he could have this, and not for them, he adds *than they,* that is, greatly differing from the name of the angels, this is the name which is above every name, namely God, or Son, which is truly worthier than that by which they are called angels, that is, messengers. For the name of Son shows what is proper, not adoption, because unless he were the proper Son, the Apostle could not from this assert the greatness of his honour. But the proper Son is begotten of the Father himself. But if he were Son by the grace of adoption, he would be less not only than the Father, but even than the angels.

notes.text: Matt. v, 31; Matt. xix, 7; Luke xvi, 18.
Deut. xxiv, 1.

From the beginning of the creation — Therefore Moses in the first of Genesis gives us an account of things from the beginning of the creation. Does it not clearly follow, that there was no creation previous to that which Moses describes? God made them male and female - Therefore Adam did not at first contain both sexes in himself: but God made Adam, when first created, male only; and Eve female only. And this man and woman he joined together, in a state of innocence, as husband and wife.
Gen. ii, 24.
All polygamy is here totally condemned.
Matt. xix, 13.

Jesus seeing it was much displeased — At their blaming those who were not blame worthy: and endeavouring to hinder the children from receiving a blessing. Of such is the kingdom of God - The members of the kingdom which I am come to set up in the world are such as these, as well as grown persons, of a child-like temper.
Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child — As totally disclaiming all worthiness and fitness, as if he were but a week old.

glossa.text: *The Pharisees asked.* Great is the distance between the crowds and the Pharisees. These come together that they may be taught, and that the sick may be healed, as Matthew plainly says: those, that by tempting they may deceive. For the devotion of piety brings these: the goad of spite leads those. *Whether it is lawful for a man to put away his wife. ((BEDA.))* He tempted him with a horned syllogism, etc., *as far as* but it was granted because of the necessity of those who sin.
*For the hardness of heart. ((ID.))* Is God contrary to himself, etc., *as far as* that the bond of wedlock should persevere through hatreds and murders.
*And they shall be,* etc. The reward of marriage is that of two there be made one flesh. Chastity joined to the spirit is made one spirit.

*Let not man put asunder.* By the desire of a second wife. God separates: he who joins, when by the consent of both, for the service of God (in that the time is short), they so have wives as though not having them.
*And in the house,* etc. ((HIER.)) It was not the disciples who asked first, etc., *as far as* that bread may strengthen the heart of man, as it is: *If any man will come after me ((Luc. IX))*, etc.

*Whosoever shall put away his wife. ((BEDA.))* Matthew more fully: *Whosoever shall put away his wife, save for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery ((Matth. V))*. There is therefore one carnal cause only, fornication: one spiritual, the fear of God, that a wife be put away, as many are read to have done for religion's sake. But no cause is prescribed by the law of God, that another be married while she lives who has been left.

*But the disciples rebuked them that brought them.* Not because they were unwilling that these should be blessed by the Saviour's hand and voice, but, not yet having full faith, they thought that after the manner of men he was wearied by the importunity of those who brought them.

*For of such is the kingdom of God.* He says "of such" with meaning, not "of these." As if he said: Manners reign, not age. The kingdom of heaven is promised to those who have the like simplicity and innocence, to whom that word to the apostles is fitting: *Be not made little ones in understanding, but in malice be little ones ((I Cor. XIV))* .

*Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom.* He who does not persevere in anger, who when hurt does not remember it, who seeing a fair woman does not covet, who has not one thing in his mouth and another in his heart. As if he said: If you shall not be such, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. *The kingdom of God.* That is, we are bidden to receive the teaching of the Gospel as little ones do, that is, as a little one does not contradict his teachers, does not frame arguments against them, but faithfully receives, obeys with fear and is quiet: so we also, obeying simply and without any contradiction, ought to receive the words of the Lord.

echoes.text: For she is a breath of the power of God, and a clear effluence of the glory of the Almighty; therefore can nothing defiled find entrance into her. For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, and an unspotted mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness. (Wisdom of Solomon 7:25–26)
echoes.note: The marquee echo of the chapter. ‘Radiance of his glory… the very image of his substance’ (v. 3) reproduces the rare term apaugasma and the eikōn/glory pairing of Wis 7:25–26 — high verbal volume against a Second Temple text most scholars (Hays, Attridge, Beale & Carson) name as the direct source. Hebrews transfers what Wisdom says of personified Sophia to the Son. Confidence kept high despite low text-field availability, since bible-api serves only the Protestant canon.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: ‘Sat down on the right hand of the Majesty’ (v. 3) is a low-volume echo of Ps 110:1, planted before the catena begins and paid off as its explicit climax at 1:13. Hays' recurrence test: the same source surfaces twice, so even the faint first instance earns credence.

echoes.text: For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh. (Leviticus 16:30)
echoes.note: ‘When he had by himself purified us of our sins’ (v. 3) quotes nothing, yet figurally invokes the Day of Atonement cult that chapters 9–10 will expound — the book's central typology. No verbal volume; high figural coherence (Hays, Reading Backwards).

echoes.text: Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was there; when he set a circle on the surface of the deep, when he established the clouds above, when the springs of the deep became strong, when he gave to the sea its boundary, that the waters should not violate his commandment, when he marked out the foundations of the earth; then I was the craftsman by his side. I was a delight day by day, always rejoicing before him, rejoicing in his whole world. My delight was with the sons of men.
echoes.note: ‘Through whom also he made the worlds’ (v. 2) draws on the Wisdom-as-agent-of-creation tradition that runs from Prov 8:22–31 into Wisdom and Sirach. Thematic coherence (Wisdom christology) more than verbal volume; the LXX of Prov 8:22 (‘the Lord created me’) fed the patristic debates this verse anticipates.

echoes.text: Ask of me, and I will give the nations for your inheritance, the uttermost parts of the earth for your possession.
echoes.note: ‘Whom he appointed heir of all things’ (v. 2) sounds the inheritance grant of Ps 2:8 — the same psalm quoted outright at 1:5. Recurrence (Hays): Ps 2 is demonstrably available and re-used, so the inheritance language is heard as its anticipatory echo.

echoes.text: Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom that which will not be destroyed.
echoes.note: ‘Heir of all things’ and the universal, unending dominion granted the one ‘like a son of man’ (Dan 7:14) share thematic coherence with the Son's inheritance and session. Faint, contested — no verbal volume — but a stock messianic substrate scholars note behind the exaltation language.

echoes.text: Yahweh, your Redeemer, and he who formed you from the womb says: ‘I am Yahweh, who makes all things; who alone stretches out the heavens; who spreads out the earth by myself;’
echoes.note: ‘Upholding all things by the word of his power’ (v. 3) ascribes to the Son the sole-creator role Isa 44:24 reserves to YHWH — a faint conceptual echo that prepares the bolder Ps 102 transfer at 1:10–12. Low volume; coherence with the creation theme of the prologue.

echoes.text: For who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh? Who among the sons of the heavenly beings is like Yahweh,
echoes.note: ‘Having become so much better than the angels’ (v. 4) faintly recalls the incomparability formula of Ps 89:6, which sets YHWH above the ‘sons of the heavenly beings.’ A dashed echo seeding the angel-comparison the catena exists to make; Ps 89 recurs at 1:6 (‘firstborn’).

echoes.text: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: Jesus grounds marriage 'from the beginning of the creation' in 'God made them male and female,' a near-verbatim citation of the creation of humanity as male and female. High Volume and explicit appeal to creation order; the phrase functions as a formal scriptural authority over against Deuteronomy's concession. Availability and Coherence are secure within Mark's argument structure.

echoes.text: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
echoes.note: The words 'a man will leave his father and mother, and will join to his wife, and the two will become one flesh' reproduce the etiological marriage saying nearly word-for-word. This is the load-bearing prooftext; Jesus stacks it on Genesis 1:27 to argue indissolubility. Maximal Volume and Recurrence in early Jewish marriage discourse.

echoes.text: When a man takes a wife and marries her, then it shall be, if she finds no favor in his eyes, because he has found some unseemly thing in her, that he shall write her a bill of divorce, and put it in her hand, and send her out of his house. When she has departed out of his house, she may go and be another man’s wife. If the latter husband hates her, and write her a bill of divorce, and puts it in her hand, and sends her out of his house; or if the latter […]
echoes.note: The 'certificate of divorce' Moses 'allowed' is a direct invocation of the Mosaic divorce statute, named explicitly as Moses' command. Jesus cites it precisely in order to subordinate it as a concession to 'hardness of heart.' Explicit attribution to Moses makes this an unambiguous, high-Volume citation.

echoes.text: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion, and the wife of your covenant. Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For I hate divorce”, says Yahweh, the God of Israel, “and him […]
echoes.note: Malachi rebukes faithless divorce, invokes 'the wife of your covenant,' appeals to the one-flesh creation ('did he not make them one?'), and reports that God 'hates divorce.' Jesus' fusion of one-flesh creation theology with a polemic against divorce coheres strongly with Malachi's distinctive argument. The shared appeal to creation against divorce raises this above generic thematic overlap.

echoes.text: He created them male and female, and blessed them. On the day they were created, he named them “Adam”.
echoes.note: The toledot restatement 'male and female he created them, and blessed them' reinforces the male-and-female creation formula Jesus cites. It is a secondary witness to the same tradition behind Genesis 1:27, strengthening Recurrence. Marked contested because Mark most plausibly draws on Genesis 1:27 directly.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “When you go back into Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the wonders which I have put in your hand, but I will harden his heart and he will not let the people go.
echoes.note: The diagnosis 'for your hardness of heart' resonates with the Pentateuch's hardened-heart vocabulary, of which the Exodus Pharaoh cycle is the paradigm. The motif frames Israel's recalcitrance as the reason for the concession. Low confidence and contested: thematic vocabulary rather than a specific citation.

echoes.text: Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn. He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads, and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham […]
echoes.note: Jacob lays his hands on Ephraim and Manasseh and blesses them, the foundational scene of patriarchal blessing by laying on of hands. Jesus 'took them in his arms, and blessed them, laying his hands on them' reenacts this gesture upon children. The verbal and ritual overlap (hands, blessing, children) gives the allusion real Volume.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him.
echoes.note: The laying on of hands to convey authority and blessing (Moses on Joshua) is the OT background for the gesture Jesus performs. It supplies the Availability of the imposition-of-hands motif. Low confidence and contested because Mark's scene is blessing, not commissioning.

echoes.text: Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.
echoes.note: The psalmist stills his soul 'like a weaned child,' modeling trustful smallness before God, which coheres with receiving the kingdom 'like a little child.' The child as image of humble dependence is the shared note. Contested and low: thematic resonance without verbal contact.

echoes.text: Better than this is childishness with virtue; For in the memory of virtue is immortality: Because it is recognized both before God and before men.
echoes.note: Wisdom prizes virtue over many children and the immortality of the righteous, part of a Second-Temple revaluation of childhood and worth. The faint resonance lies in valuing what the world overlooks, as the disciples overlook the children. Contested; included for maximal coverage of deuterocanonical availability.

notes.text: This was done upon the sixth day, as was also the placing of Adam in paradise, though it be here mentioned after an account of the seventh day's rest: but what was said in general, chap. i, 27, that God made man male and female is more distinctly related here, God caused the sleep to fall on Adam, and made it a deep sleep, that so the opening of his side might be no grievance to him: while he knows no sin, God will take care he shall feel no pain. See note at "ver. 21"

And Adam said, this is now bone of my bones — Probably it was revealed to Adam in a vision, when he was asleep, that this lovely creature, now presented to him, was a piece of himself and was to be his companion, and the wife of his covenant - In token of his acceptance of her, he gave her a name, not peculiar to her, but common to her sex; she shall be called woman, Isha, a She- man, differing from man in sex only, not in nature; made of man, and joined to man.

The sabbath and marriage were two ordinances instituted in innocency, the former for the preservation of the church, the latter for the preservation of mankind. It appears by Matt. xix, 4, 5, that it was God himself who said here, a man must leave all his relations to cleave to his wife; but whether he spake it by Moses or by Adam who spake, ver. 23 is uncertain: It should seem they are the words of Adam in God's name, laying down this law to all his posterity. The virtue of a divine ordinance, and the bonds of it, are stronger even than those of nature. See how necessary it is that children should take their parents consent with them in their marriage; and how unjust they are to their parents, as well as undutiful, if they marry without it; for they rob them of their right to them, and interest in them, and alienate it to another fraudulently and unnaturally.

glossa.text: « The Lord also said, » etc. ((AUG., l. IX de Gen., c. 8.)) Those who hold that it was not lawful to have intercourse in paradise for the begetting of children, etc., *as far as* soul from soul, or in whatever other way the soul comes to be.

« He brought them, » etc. ((AUG., l. IX de Gen. ad litt., c. 14, tom. III.)) Not as hunters do, or fowlers; nor was there a voice of command made out of a cloud, such as rational souls are wont to understand; for this beasts or birds do not naturally understand, etc., *as far as* they are understood to have been created of earth.

((HIERON.)) It seems that the first language of the human race was Hebrew, because the names which we read in Genesis until the division of tongues are agreed to be of that language.

« And he called, » etc. ((AUG.)) *Mystically.* Signifying the Gentiles who should be saved in the Church through Christ, and should receive the name of Christ, which before they did not have; whence, Isa. LXV: « I will call my servants by another name. »

« But for Adam there was not found, » etc. ((AUG., lib. IX de Gen. ad litt., cap. 15 et seq.)) It must be seen how the forming of the woman was made, which is mystically called a building, etc., *as far as* that we may understand that through that ecstasy Adam said these things by God's gift.

 « But for Adam there was not found a helper. » No faithful just man can be made equal to Christ. Psalm XLIV: « For he is beautiful in form above the sons of men. » For no one could deliver the human race but himself. Whence Apocalypse V: « No one was found worthy to open the book and to loose the seals thereof, » etc.

« But for Adam there was not found, » etc. ((AUG., de Gen. contra Manich., l. II, c. 13.)) The woman was made for the help of the man, etc., *as far as* and to subjugate to the dominion of reason, grace cooperating.

« The Lord therefore cast, » etc. *((ISID. ex Aug., ut supra, c. 13, 14.)) Mystically.* These things cannot be seen with bodily eyes. But the further a man withdraws from things visible to the secrets of understanding, as it were by falling asleep, the better and more sincerely he sees, etc., *as far as* and to be referred to the Church.

((AUG., lib. X de Gen. ad litt., c. I.)) Those who think that the soul is from a soul, etc., *as far as* which had been said of the man.

((AUG., ibid., c. 19, 20.)) If it be asked whence Christ received his soul, I would rather hear men better and more learned; etc., *as far as* to whom what answer might be made has not yet occurred to me.

« The Lord therefore cast a deep sleep, » etc. ((GREG., Moral., l. XXX, tom. II.)) We do not attain the summit of contemplation, if we do not cease from the oppression of outward care: nor do we look upon our own selves, so as to know that there is in us one thing rational which rules, another animal which is ruled, unless, betaking ourselves to the secret of silence, we are lulled asleep from outward disturbance. Which Adam well figured in his sleeping, from whose side the woman presently came forth. For he who is caught up to the understanding of inward things closes his eyes to visible things, and then understands that there is in himself one thing which ought to rule, as a man; another which should be ruled, as a woman.

« And he built. . . . Wherefore a man shall leave, » etc. ((ISID., in Gen., t. V.)) What was fulfilled in Adam according to the history, etc., *as far as* For the serpent prefigures the poisons of heretics.

notes.text: In — Not only in Israel, but among all nations. Which shews that this psalm speaks of the Messiah, and the times of the New Testament. Heavens - Where thy throne of glory is established, where the blessed angels celebrate thy praises, where Christ sitteth at thy right hand in glorious majesty, from whence he poureth down excellent gifts upon babes.

Babes — Weak and foolish, and contemptible persons, who are frequently called babes or children. Such are very unfit to grapple with an enemy: and therefore when such persons conquer the most powerful and malicious enemies, it must needs confound them, and advance the glory of God: as indeed it did, when such mean persons as the apostles, and disciples of Christ, maintained and propagated the gospel, in spite of all the wit, power, and rage of their enemies. Ordained - Perfectly or firmly settled strength; that is, the praise of his strength or power, Matt. xxi, 16, it is rendered praise. Still - Silence and confound them. Avenger - The devil, and all who are his vassals and espouse his quarrel.

The moon — Either the sun is included under this general title: or he omitted it, because he made this psalm by night. Ordained - Placed in that excellent and unalterable order, and directed to their several motions.

What is man — How mean and inconsiderable a thing is man, if compared with thy glorious majesty. Man - Hebrew. infirm, or miserable man. By which it is apparent that he speaks of man, not according to the state of his creation, but as fallen into a state of sin and misery, and mortality. Mindful - Carest for him, and conferest such high favours upon him. The son - Hebrew. the son of Adam, that great apostate from God, the sinful son of a sinful father, his son by likeness of disposition and manners, no less than by procreation. All which tends to magnify the following mercy. Visitest - Not in anger, as that word is sometimes used, but with thy grace and mercy.

For — Thou hast in Christ mercifully restored man to his primitive estate, wherein he was but one remove below the angels; from which he was fallen by sin. Crowned - Man, fallen and lost man: who is actually restored to glory and dominion in Christ his head and representative, who received this crown and dominion for man's good, and in his stead; which he will in due time communicate to his members. And so the two expositions of this place concerning mankind and concerning Christ, may be reconciled. For he speaks of that honourable estate conferred first upon Christ, and then by his hands upon mankind. But the words more literally rendered are, Thou madest him a little less than God. And hence some have inferred, that man in his original state was the highest of all creatures. David praises God for giving him victory over his enemies, ver. 1-6. Triumphs in confidence that God would judge the world and protect his people, ver. 7-10. Calls others to praise him, ver. 11, 12. Prays for help, and praises God, ver. 13-20. To the chief musician upon Muth-labben, A psalm of David Title of the psalm. Muth-labben - This also seems to be a title of some tune, or instrument: of which we may be content to be ignorant, as the Jewish doctors are.

glossa.text: « O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is thy name! etc. » ((CASS.)) First the praises of God, his majesty, and his exalted working are described. « In the whole. » ((Ibid.)) Let not the Jews therefore, or any others, claim for themselves what belongs to all, which is the intent. « Above the heavens. » ((AUG.)) Literally, or the Scriptures: because it exceeds the utterances of all the Scriptures; or, « above the heavens. » Continuing with what follows, that is, into the Scriptures, which he bends down to babes, on account of the enemies of the cross: who are destroyed, when the Scriptures are seen, that is, understood, to be led down as far as babes: and when through them they are nourished unto strength, and are raised to the sublimity of understanding.

« Out of the mouth of infants. » ((Ibid.)) Of the unwise, to whom the Apostle gave milk, whom those signified who praised the Lord, in whom the Lord uses this testimony. Out of these he hath perfected praise, because if only the perfect were in the Church, no counsel would be taken for the human race; as now, when even the least, not yet capable of the knowledge of spiritual things, are nourished by faith in the history of things temporal. « Enemies » are all who speak things contrary to the dispensation made through the Crucified. « Defenders » the heretics seem of the faith, the philosophers of wisdom, although yet the former impugn the faith, and the latter true wisdom. « Sucklings, » ((CASS.)) not in age, but as Peter has it, « as newborn babes ((I Petr. II)), » who cannot yet take food, but milk; and it is: thou art proclaimed not only by the perfect, but also by the unwise. Or, he calls infants and sucklings the apostles, who were simple and unlearned men; whence: « The foolish things of the world « God hath chosen, that he may confound the strong ((I Cor. I)). » The praise is more perfect. Or, out of the mouth of infants and sucklings, that is, out of the words of the Hebrew children thou hast perfected praise, which seemed to be done childishly, on account of the enemies, that it might not seem to be human wisdom, but divinely given. « Thine enemies. » The pagans. « The enemy. » The Jew, who is an enemy of God, while he defends the Father alone: because « he that honoureth not the Son, honoureth not « the Father, » or an enemy in his will.

« For I shall see. » Before the Jew, in spirit. « Thy heavens, » the apostles, I shall see present in their descendants; this well suits those of the first age. « The works of thy fingers. » Because they are perfected by the cooperation of the Trinity, which is signified here in the three fingers, as there: « Who weigheth the bulk of the earth with three fingers. » ((Isa. XL.)) And through them, « The moon and the stars which thou hast founded. » Not they.

« What is man. » ((Ibid.)) Secondly, he says that the nature of man, once corrupted, is exalted in Christ above all things. For before he had shown the omnipotence of the Godhead. By man, sinners; by the son of man, the spiritual. ((Ibid.)) Man, any vile person, of whom God is mindful in showing mercy, the Son of man, Christ as man: since through him thou visitest him, when the Word was made flesh, in which the physician came to the sick. « Or the son. » ((AUG.)) The disjunction hints that there is a distance between man and the son of man. Every son of man is man, but not conversely, as Adam. Every man therefore, who bears the image of the earthly: the Son of man, who is heavenly, and deservedly a new man, son of man: because the new is made out of the old by a certain change. ((AUG.)) Why, leaving the higher things, does he speak of these lowest ones? But the sheep, etc., *as far as* who by the seed of the word of God make the hearts of men to bear fruit.

« Moreover the cattle also. » He notes therefore that the wicked also are subject to Christ, which seems less: for these carnal men dwell in the breadth of the plain, that is, in the amplitude of pleasures, not in the mountains of virtues. « The cattle of the field. » ((Ibid.)) Who live in the flesh, where they climb nothing steep: but the broad way, to which they cling, is that which leads to destruction: whence also Abel is slain in the field.

« The birds, » the proud: of whom, « They have set their mouth against heaven ((Psal. LXXII)). » Whose head says: « I will ascend into heaven, and I will exalt my throne, and I will be like the Most High ((Isa. XIV)). « The fishes of the sea that walk through the paths of the sea, » the curious. These three, the pleasure of the flesh, pride, curiosity, include all vices, which are the concupiscence of the flesh, the ambition of the world, that is, pride, the concupiscence of the eyes, since through the eyes curiosity chiefly prevails.

notes.text: The proposition and sum, 5-9

The treatise itself. We have a perfect author of salvation, who suffered for our sake, that he might be, (1.) a merciful, and (2.) a faithful, (3.) high priest,. 10-13 These three are particularly explained, his passion and consummation being continually interwoven

1. He has the virtues of an high priest a. He is faithful, iii.1 Therefore be ye not unfaithful iv.13 b. He is merciful, 15 Therefore come to him with confidence v.3

2. He is called of God an high priest. Here, a. The sum is proposed, 4-10 With a summary exhortation 11- vi. 20 b. The point is copiously,

1. Explained. We have a great high priest,

1. Such as is described in the hundred and tenth Psalm After the order of Melchisedec, vii. 1-19 Established by an oath, 20-22 For ever, 23-28

2. Therefore peculiarly excellent-Heavenly, viii. 1-6 Of the new covenant, 7-13 By whom we have an entrance into the sanctuary ix. 1 x. 18

2. Applied. Therefore,

1. Believe, hope, love 19-25 These three are farther inculcated, a. Faith, with patience, 26-39 Which, after the example of the ancients,. xi.1 xii.1 And of Christ himself, 2, 3 Is to be exercised, 4-11 Cheerfully, peaceably, holily, 12-17 b. Hope, 18-20 c. Love, C.xiii. 1-6

2. In order to grow in these graces, make use of The remembrance of your former, 7-16 The vigilance of your present, pastors, 17-19 To this period, and to the whole epistle, answers The prayer, the doxology, and the mild conclusion, 20-25 There are many comparisons in this epistle, which may be nearly reduced to two heads:

1. The prophets, the angels, Moses, Joshua, Aaron, are great; but Jesus Christ is infinitely greater

2. The ancient believers enjoyed high privileges; but Christian believers enjoy far higher. To illustrate this, examples both of happiness and misery are everywhere interspersed: so that in this epistle there is a kind of recapitulation of the whole Old Testament. In this also Judaism is abrogated, and Christianity carried to its height. HEBREWS

Who sat down — The third of these glorious predicates, with which three other particulars are interwoven, which are mentioned likewise, and in the same order, Colossians i, 15, 17, 20. Who, being - The glory which he received in his exaltation at the right hand of the Father no angel was capable of; but the Son alone, who likewise enjoyed it long before. The brightness of his glory - Glory is the nature of God revealed in its brightness. The express image - Or stamp. Whatever the Father is, is exhibited in the Son, as a seal in the stamp on wax. Of his person - Or substance. The word denotes the unchangeable perpetuity of divine life and power. And sustaining all things - Visible and invisible, in being. By the word of his power - That is, by his powerful word. When he had by himself - Without any Mosaic rites or ceremonies. Purged our sins - In order to which it was necessary he should for a time divest himself of his glory. In this chapter St. Paul describes his glory chiefly as he is the Son of God; afterwards, ver. 6, &c., the glory of the man Christ Jesus. He speaks, indeed, briefly of the former before his humiliation, but copiously after his exaltation; as from hence the glory he had from eternity began to be evidently seen. Both his purging our sins, and sitting on the right hand of God, are largely treated of in the seven following chapters. Sat down - The priests stood while they ministered: sitting, therefore, denotes the consummation of his sacrifice. This word, sat down, contains the scope, the theme, and the sum, of the epistle.

This verse has two clauses, the latter of which is treated of, ver. 5; the former, ver. 13. Such transpositions are also found in the other epistles of St. Paul, but in none so frequently as in this. The Jewish doctors were peculiarly fond of this figure, and used it much in all their writings. The apostle therefore, becoming all things to all men, here follows the same method. All the inspired writers were readier in all the figures of speech than the most experienced orators. Being — By his exaltation, after he had been lower than them, chap. ii, 9. So much higher than the angels - It was extremely proper to observe this, because the Jews gloried in their law, as it was delivered by the ministration of angels. How much more may we glory in the gospel, which was given, not by the ministry of angels, but of the very Son of God! As he hath by inheritance a more excellent name - Because he is the Son of God, he inherits that name, in right whereof he inherits all things His inheriting that name is more ancient than all worlds; his inheriting all things, as ancient as all things. Than they - This denotes an immense preeminence. The angels do not inherit all things, but are themselves a portion of the Son's inheritance, whom they worship as their Lord.

glossa.text: *Of old.* It is not new. *God,* who is unchangeable then and now. *Speaking.* He says: *speaking,* in the present, because what was then is even now. *To the fathers.* That is, to those who are fathers to us in flesh and in the worship of God. *In the prophets.* For not they themselves, but God in them. *In divers manners.* That is, many times to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the rest, and often to the same men. *And in many ways.* Because now by dreams, as to Daniel: now by an open voice, as to Moses: now by inward inspiration, as to David.

*In the Son,* who is greater than the prophets. For he is the fulfiller and sanctifier of the prophets. Thus then he is a prophet, in that he is also the Lord of the prophets. So too Christ is an angel, in that he is also the Lord of the angels. *He appointed* unchangeably. *Heir of all things,* that is, possessor of every creature. For Jacob is no longer the portion of the Lord, and Israel his part: but absolutely all the nations of the world.

*Who being the brightness of his glory,* etc. Here he commends Christ according to his divine nature, showing him coeternal and coequal with the Father, and of the same substance with him, but other in person.

*The figure of his substance.* Behold, otherwise, personally, as a figure from him whose figure it is. But equal, because not unlike, as he himself says: *The Father is in me;* and: *He that seeth me, seeth my Father also ((Joan. XIV))*. Note that these names, namely light, glory, are sometimes referred to the divine nature, sometimes to the person. And when they are referred to the person; they are referred now to the Father, now to the Son. For we say: The Father is light, and the Son is light. Likewise the Father is glory, the Son glory, and these two are one glory and one light, not two. And the Son is called glory of glory, as light of light, and beginning of beginning, and God of God, yet not two gods, but one, not two beginnings, but one. But brightness and figure, as image also, are properly referred to the person of the Son and are said relatively.

 *And upholding all things,* etc. It was said above that through him he made all things. Here he now attributes to him the sum of authority, from this, that with authority he governs and holds together all things. For as all things were created by him, so through him, who is unchangeable, they are preserved. For the omnipotence of the Creator is the cause of subsisting to every creature, and if that power should at any time cease from ruling the things it founded, at once the form and nature of all things would fall together.

*Purgation.* After he has shown the excellence of him by whom he created and governs all things, here he commends the kindness of his humility. For he puts us in mind of the cross and the resurrection and the ascension, where he says: *He sitteth,* etc. *On high.* In saying this, he does not shut God up in a place: but shows the man Christ loftier than all and more eminent than all. So also by the right hand he did not give God a shape, but showed the likeness of honour. For he that hath confessed *Confessus*; read *consessus*, "the sitting together" shows nothing else but equality of honour.

*So much better.* Yet in the psalm he says: *He was made a little less than the angels ((Psal. VIII))*. Here he is said to be better than the same. And as that was said according to his human nature, so this too could be understood to have been said according to the divine, were it not that *made* is added, by which it is opened that here he speaks of him according to the flesh. For according to that whereby he is acknowledged consubstantial with the substance of the Father, he was not made, but born: the discourse therefore is of him according to his human nature, according to which he was both less than the angels in his passion, and greater and better also in the fulness of grace, of which the angels themselves also receive by measure.

*A more differing name.* While he was mortal, he had a differing name, because the angels ministered to him. After he was immortal, more differing still. And because he could have this, and not for them, he adds *than they,* that is, greatly differing from the name of the angels, this is the name which is above every name, namely God, or Son, which is truly worthier than that by which they are called angels, that is, messengers. For the name of Son shows what is proper, not adoption, because unless he were the proper Son, the Apostle could not from this assert the greatness of his honour. But the proper Son is begotten of the Father himself. But if he were Son by the grace of adoption, he would be less not only than the Father, but even than the angels.

notes.text: Matt. v, 31; Matt. xix, 7; Luke xvi, 18.
Deut. xxiv, 1.

From the beginning of the creation — Therefore Moses in the first of Genesis gives us an account of things from the beginning of the creation. Does it not clearly follow, that there was no creation previous to that which Moses describes? God made them male and female - Therefore Adam did not at first contain both sexes in himself: but God made Adam, when first created, male only; and Eve female only. And this man and woman he joined together, in a state of innocence, as husband and wife.
Gen. ii, 24.
All polygamy is here totally condemned.
Matt. xix, 13.

Jesus seeing it was much displeased — At their blaming those who were not blame worthy: and endeavouring to hinder the children from receiving a blessing. Of such is the kingdom of God - The members of the kingdom which I am come to set up in the world are such as these, as well as grown persons, of a child-like temper.
Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child — As totally disclaiming all worthiness and fitness, as if he were but a week old.

glossa.text: *The Pharisees asked.* Great is the distance between the crowds and the Pharisees. These come together that they may be taught, and that the sick may be healed, as Matthew plainly says: those, that by tempting they may deceive. For the devotion of piety brings these: the goad of spite leads those. *Whether it is lawful for a man to put away his wife. ((BEDA.))* He tempted him with a horned syllogism, etc., *as far as* but it was granted because of the necessity of those who sin.
*For the hardness of heart. ((ID.))* Is God contrary to himself, etc., *as far as* that the bond of wedlock should persevere through hatreds and murders.
*And they shall be,* etc. The reward of marriage is that of two there be made one flesh. Chastity joined to the spirit is made one spirit.

*Let not man put asunder.* By the desire of a second wife. God separates: he who joins, when by the consent of both, for the service of God (in that the time is short), they so have wives as though not having them.
*And in the house,* etc. ((HIER.)) It was not the disciples who asked first, etc., *as far as* that bread may strengthen the heart of man, as it is: *If any man will come after me ((Luc. IX))*, etc.

*Whosoever shall put away his wife. ((BEDA.))* Matthew more fully: *Whosoever shall put away his wife, save for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery ((Matth. V))*. There is therefore one carnal cause only, fornication: one spiritual, the fear of God, that a wife be put away, as many are read to have done for religion's sake. But no cause is prescribed by the law of God, that another be married while she lives who has been left.

*But the disciples rebuked them that brought them.* Not because they were unwilling that these should be blessed by the Saviour's hand and voice, but, not yet having full faith, they thought that after the manner of men he was wearied by the importunity of those who brought them.

*For of such is the kingdom of God.* He says "of such" with meaning, not "of these." As if he said: Manners reign, not age. The kingdom of heaven is promised to those who have the like simplicity and innocence, to whom that word to the apostles is fitting: *Be not made little ones in understanding, but in malice be little ones ((I Cor. XIV))* .

*Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom.* He who does not persevere in anger, who when hurt does not remember it, who seeing a fair woman does not covet, who has not one thing in his mouth and another in his heart. As if he said: If you shall not be such, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. *The kingdom of God.* That is, we are bidden to receive the teaching of the Gospel as little ones do, that is, as a little one does not contradict his teachers, does not frame arguments against them, but faithfully receives, obeys with fear and is quiet: so we also, obeying simply and without any contradiction, ought to receive the words of the Lord.

echoes.text: For she is a breath of the power of God, and a clear effluence of the glory of the Almighty; therefore can nothing defiled find entrance into her. For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, and an unspotted mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness. (Wisdom of Solomon 7:25–26)
echoes.note: The marquee echo of the chapter. ‘Radiance of his glory… the very image of his substance’ (v. 3) reproduces the rare term apaugasma and the eikōn/glory pairing of Wis 7:25–26 — high verbal volume against a Second Temple text most scholars (Hays, Attridge, Beale & Carson) name as the direct source. Hebrews transfers what Wisdom says of personified Sophia to the Son. Confidence kept high despite low text-field availability, since bible-api serves only the Protestant canon.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: ‘Sat down on the right hand of the Majesty’ (v. 3) is a low-volume echo of Ps 110:1, planted before the catena begins and paid off as its explicit climax at 1:13. Hays' recurrence test: the same source surfaces twice, so even the faint first instance earns credence.

echoes.text: For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before Yahweh. (Leviticus 16:30)
echoes.note: ‘When he had by himself purified us of our sins’ (v. 3) quotes nothing, yet figurally invokes the Day of Atonement cult that chapters 9–10 will expound — the book's central typology. No verbal volume; high figural coherence (Hays, Reading Backwards).

echoes.text: Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born; while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world. When he established the heavens, I was there; when he set a circle on the surface of the deep, when he established the clouds above, when the springs of the deep became strong, when he gave to the sea its boundary, that the waters should not violate his commandment, when he marked out the foundations of the earth; then I was the craftsman by his side. I was a delight day by day, always rejoicing before him, rejoicing in his whole world. My delight was with the sons of men.
echoes.note: ‘Through whom also he made the worlds’ (v. 2) draws on the Wisdom-as-agent-of-creation tradition that runs from Prov 8:22–31 into Wisdom and Sirach. Thematic coherence (Wisdom christology) more than verbal volume; the LXX of Prov 8:22 (‘the Lord created me’) fed the patristic debates this verse anticipates.

echoes.text: Ask of me, and I will give the nations for your inheritance, the uttermost parts of the earth for your possession.
echoes.note: ‘Whom he appointed heir of all things’ (v. 2) sounds the inheritance grant of Ps 2:8 — the same psalm quoted outright at 1:5. Recurrence (Hays): Ps 2 is demonstrably available and re-used, so the inheritance language is heard as its anticipatory echo.

echoes.text: Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom that which will not be destroyed.
echoes.note: ‘Heir of all things’ and the universal, unending dominion granted the one ‘like a son of man’ (Dan 7:14) share thematic coherence with the Son's inheritance and session. Faint, contested — no verbal volume — but a stock messianic substrate scholars note behind the exaltation language.

echoes.text: Yahweh, your Redeemer, and he who formed you from the womb says: ‘I am Yahweh, who makes all things; who alone stretches out the heavens; who spreads out the earth by myself;’
echoes.note: ‘Upholding all things by the word of his power’ (v. 3) ascribes to the Son the sole-creator role Isa 44:24 reserves to YHWH — a faint conceptual echo that prepares the bolder Ps 102 transfer at 1:10–12. Low volume; coherence with the creation theme of the prologue.

echoes.text: For who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh? Who among the sons of the heavenly beings is like Yahweh,
echoes.note: ‘Having become so much better than the angels’ (v. 4) faintly recalls the incomparability formula of Ps 89:6, which sets YHWH above the ‘sons of the heavenly beings.’ A dashed echo seeding the angel-comparison the catena exists to make; Ps 89 recurs at 1:6 (‘firstborn’).

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: Jesus grounds marriage 'from the beginning of the creation' in 'God made them male and female,' a near-verbatim citation of the creation of humanity as male and female. High Volume and explicit appeal to creation order; the phrase functions as a formal scriptural authority over against Deuteronomy's concession. Availability and Coherence are secure within Mark's argument structure.

echoes.text: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
echoes.note: The words 'a man will leave his father and mother, and will join to his wife, and the two will become one flesh' reproduce the etiological marriage saying nearly word-for-word. This is the load-bearing prooftext; Jesus stacks it on Genesis 1:27 to argue indissolubility. Maximal Volume and Recurrence in early Jewish marriage discourse.

echoes.text: When a man takes a wife and marries her, then it shall be, if she finds no favor in his eyes, because he has found some unseemly thing in her, that he shall write her a bill of divorce, and put it in her hand, and send her out of his house. When she has departed out of his house, she may go and be another man’s wife. If the latter husband hates her, and write her a bill of divorce, and puts it in her hand, and sends her out of his house; or if the latter […]
echoes.note: The 'certificate of divorce' Moses 'allowed' is a direct invocation of the Mosaic divorce statute, named explicitly as Moses' command. Jesus cites it precisely in order to subordinate it as a concession to 'hardness of heart.' Explicit attribution to Moses makes this an unambiguous, high-Volume citation.

echoes.text: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion, and the wife of your covenant. Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For I hate divorce”, says Yahweh, the God of Israel, “and him […]
echoes.note: Malachi rebukes faithless divorce, invokes 'the wife of your covenant,' appeals to the one-flesh creation ('did he not make them one?'), and reports that God 'hates divorce.' Jesus' fusion of one-flesh creation theology with a polemic against divorce coheres strongly with Malachi's distinctive argument. The shared appeal to creation against divorce raises this above generic thematic overlap.

echoes.text: He created them male and female, and blessed them. On the day they were created, he named them “Adam”.
echoes.note: The toledot restatement 'male and female he created them, and blessed them' reinforces the male-and-female creation formula Jesus cites. It is a secondary witness to the same tradition behind Genesis 1:27, strengthening Recurrence. Marked contested because Mark most plausibly draws on Genesis 1:27 directly.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “When you go back into Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the wonders which I have put in your hand, but I will harden his heart and he will not let the people go.
echoes.note: The diagnosis 'for your hardness of heart' resonates with the Pentateuch's hardened-heart vocabulary, of which the Exodus Pharaoh cycle is the paradigm. The motif frames Israel's recalcitrance as the reason for the concession. Low confidence and contested: thematic vocabulary rather than a specific citation.

echoes.text: Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn. He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads, and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham […]
echoes.note: Jacob lays his hands on Ephraim and Manasseh and blesses them, the foundational scene of patriarchal blessing by laying on of hands. Jesus 'took them in his arms, and blessed them, laying his hands on them' reenacts this gesture upon children. The verbal and ritual overlap (hands, blessing, children) gives the allusion real Volume.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him.
echoes.note: The laying on of hands to convey authority and blessing (Moses on Joshua) is the OT background for the gesture Jesus performs. It supplies the Availability of the imposition-of-hands motif. Low confidence and contested because Mark's scene is blessing, not commissioning.

echoes.text: Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.
echoes.note: The psalmist stills his soul 'like a weaned child,' modeling trustful smallness before God, which coheres with receiving the kingdom 'like a little child.' The child as image of humble dependence is the shared note. Contested and low: thematic resonance without verbal contact.

echoes.text: Better than this is childishness with virtue; For in the memory of virtue is immortality: Because it is recognized both before God and before men.
echoes.note: Wisdom prizes virtue over many children and the immortality of the righteous, part of a Second-Temple revaluation of childhood and worth. The faint resonance lies in valuing what the world overlooks, as the disciples overlook the children. Contested; included for maximal coverage of deuterocanonical availability.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

registers.label: Spare
lines: When we look at the heavens, the moon and stars you set in place —
what are we, that you would care for us?
Yet you crown us with glory and honor.
You take us up in your arms.
Let the children come; do not stop them.
The kingdom belongs to such as these.
Come, let us worship with empty hands.
We come like children. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: When Jesus saw them keeping the little ones away he was indignant: Let the children come to me. And he took them up in his arms and blessed them.
We come to you like children.
For this is how the kingdom is received — not earned, not bought, but opened to like a gift placed in small and trusting hands.
We come to you like children.
What are we, that you are mindful of us? Yet you crown us with glory; you call us your own.
We come to you like children.
So come without your defenses, come without your résumé. There is a blessing here for you.
We come to you like children. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Jesus took the little ones up in his arms.
We come like children.
The kingdom belongs to such as these.
We come like children.
What are we, that you should care for us?
We come like children.
Come with open hands and be blessed.
We come like children. Amen.
